gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many external screens each MacBook drives on its own: Apple lists one for the M2 MacBook Air, the M3 MacBook Air with its lid open and the MacBook Neo, and two for the M4 and M5 MacBook Air. So a dual or triple extender, which is two or three external displays to macOS, extends on those one-display Macs only through extra display software, while a single portable monitor works on all of them.
standout_why: I compared against the two cited pages and one top result. ViewSonic's dual-screen guide (cited) says only that its stacked dual-screen feature 'is unavailable on macOS and mobile devices due to MST limitations over USB-C' and that 'only the lower display activates'. bestusefultips (cited) says 'Mac display limits depend on the exact Apple silicon generation and model' and 'Do not assume a laptop that can drive one external monitor can automatically drive two', but names no chip and no count. The Best Buy Canada page (cited) returned only navigation text in the first 100,000 characters I read, with nothing on video paths. ChatGPT's own answer says only 'MacBook users should also verify external-display limits'. None of them gives Apple's count for each chip or says that a single added screen avoids the limit.
decides: The answer to 'is an extender better than a portable monitor' depends on the laptop. On an M1 or M2 MacBook Air, an M3 MacBook Air with the lid open, or a MacBook Neo, Apple supports only one external display. A dual or triple extender then needs the maker's display software: Macworld says plain M1 and M2 Macs and the Neo need a free download 'rather like DisplayLink'. A single portable monitor, or a one-screen attachable like the Duex Max DS over USB-C Alt Mode, works natively. On an M4 or M5 MacBook Air (two external displays per Apple), or with two DP-capable USB-C ports as Mobile Pixels' manual asks, the Trio 3 Pro runs both screens with no driver. That makes the extender a real option there. So for base-chip Macs the finding backs ChatGPT's 'portable monitor' lean, and for M4/M5 and Pro/Max Macs it removes the compatibility objection to a dual extender.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air (M2, 2022)
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (M2, 2022) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's wording: 'One external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz.' A two-screen extender is two external displays, so this Mac extends only one of them natively.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air (13-inch, M3, 2024)
findings.value: 1 external display with the lid open; a second only with the lid closed (up to 5K at 60 Hz)
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (13-inch, M3, 2024) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple: 'One external display with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz' and 'Close the MacBook Air lid to use a second external display with up to 5K resolution at 60Hz.' An extender is used with the lid open, so the base M3 Air natively drives one added screen.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air (13-inch, M4, 2025)
findings.value: up to 2 external displays (up to 6K at 60 Hz) alongside the built-in display
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (13-inch, M4, 2025) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple: 'Simultaneously supports full native resolution on the built-in display at 1 billion colors and: Up to two external displays with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz.'

findings.label: External displays, current MacBook Air (M5)
findings.value: up to 2 external displays, including 2 over a single Thunderbolt port, alongside the built-in display
findings.source_title: MacBook Air 13- and 15-inch - Tech Specs - Apple
findings.note: Apple: 'Supports up to two external displays' and 'Supports up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port' and 'Simultaneously supports the built-in display at full native resolution.' Chip on the page: Apple M5.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Neo
findings.note: Apple A18 Pro chip. Apple: 'Supports one external display with up to a native resolution of 4K at 60Hz.'

findings.label: Video path for the two screens
findings.value: one USB-C cable per screen; no driver if the laptop has two DP-enabled USB-C ports; plain M1/M2 Macs and the MacBook Neo need Mobile Pixels' free display software
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review: MacBook's dual QHD screen wingspan (Macworld, Simon Jary, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Simon Jary (Macworld): 'The screens connect to the MacBook with the included two USB-C cables'. He quotes the manual: no driver needed with 'two DP enabled USB-C ports'. Plain M1 and M2 Macs and the Neo are 'limited to connecting just a single monitor' and need free software 'rather like DisplayLink'. 'An M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max or any M4/M5 MacBook should be fine.' He does not name the base M3 directly, but Apple's M3 spec page puts it at one external display with the lid open, so it falls in the software-needed group.

ViewSonic: 'This feature is unavailable on macOS and mobile devices due to MST limitations over USB-C' and 'Only the lower display activates when extending on these devices.' Listed here to show what the rival already covers: the MST limit, but not Apple's count for each chip.
